title: CA Parent & Youth Helpline
source_name: California Parent & Youth Helpline website (page updated 2026-10-22); California Health and Human Services suicide prevention resources page
source_says: California Parent & Youth Helpline ... calls, texts, and live chats 24/7 ... is at risk of shutting down entirely.
steps: Searched the helpline name and number. Opened the helpline's own site: name "California Parent & Youth Helpline", number 855-427-2736, footer "(c)2026", page modified 2026-10-22, with a notice that budget cuts put it at risk. Name and number match the app. Hours disagree across sources, and the app prints none: own site says 24/7; parentsanonymous.org/helpline/another-helpline says "12 hours a day, 7 days a week, 8AM-10PM" (page from 2024); chhs.ca.gov lists "CA Parent and Youth Help Line", "Call 855-427-2736", "Operating Hours: 8am - 8pm" (page from 2023); cdss.ca.gov OCAP Parent Resources lists "Parents Anonymous Parent and Youth Helpline" with a nine-digit number. News: NBC Palm Springs, 2026-05-16, "People can still call the National Parent Youth Helpline at 855-427-2736" and a "40% abandonment rate"; IECN, 2026-10-08, says the line is "on the brink of closure" with no state money this year. I could not place a test call, so "working today" rests on the site updated 2026-10-22. Pages were read through the web fetch tool, which returns short quoted segments.
fix: California Parent & Youth Helpline: call or text 1-855-427-2736. Waits can be long. Do not print hours, because the sources do not agree. The line says it may shut down, so have a person call it before each release.

title: Adjudication
statement: The hearing where the judge decides if the allegations in the petition are true (also called adjudication). (glossary_terms, Jurisdiction Hearing, definition)
source_name: California Courts Self-Help Guide for parents; Judicial Council booklet "Juvenile Dependency Court and You"; Judicial Council caregivers booklet; rule 5.684; courts.ca.gov dependency flow chart
source_says: This is when the judge will decide whether the allegations in the petition are true.
steps: Looked for any California court source that puts "adjudication" next to the jurisdiction hearing. Opened nine: the Self-Help Guide for parents, the booklet (it says "that is why the hearing is called the jurisdictional hearing"), the caregivers booklet, rule 5.684, the courts.ca.gov dependency flow chart ("JURISDICTIONAL HEARING §355"), the Dependency Quick Guide contents page, and the San Bernardino, Orange and Sacramento court pages. None uses "adjudication" for this hearing. A training handout on courts.ca.gov (btb25-preconjdlp-01.pdf) uses the word for a different step, under the disposition hearing: "must determine whether the child should be adjudicated a dependent of the court." The Dependency Quick Guide PDF itself would not open. Pages were read through the web fetch tool, which returns short quoted segments.
fix: The hearing where the judge decides if the allegations in the petition are true. It is also called the jurisdictional hearing.

title: Juvenile court law code range
statement: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code §§ 200-395 (legal_content, California Welfare and Institutions Code (WIC), legal_reference)
source_name: WIC Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 2 table of contents; WIC 200
source_says: CHAPTER 2 - Juvenile Court Law ... ARTICLE 6 - Dependent Children—Jurisdiction (300-304.7) ... ARTICLE 13 - Dependent Children—Appeals (395)
steps: Searched "Arnold-Kennick Juvenile Court Law chapter 2 section 200", opened the Justia table of contents for the chapter and the public.law page for section 200 ("This chapter shall be known and may be cited as the "Arnold-Kennick Juvenile Court Law.""). The Juvenile Court Law is the whole chapter: Article 1, General Provisions, starts at 200 and Article 28 ends at 987. The articles named "Dependent Children" are Articles 6 to 13, sections 300 to 395. Notices in dependency cases are Article 5.5, sections 290.1 to 297. Wards (delinquency) start at 601. So 200 to 395 is not the full Juvenile Court Law, but it does hold the general rules plus every dependency article, which is what the entry uses it for. Dependency rules also sit outside that span, for example 827 (records) and 16501.1 (case plans), both opened in this run. Pages were read through the web fetch tool, which returns short quoted segments.
fix: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code sections 200 to 395. Dependency cases are sections 300 to 395. Do not call 200 to 395 "the Juvenile Court Law", because that law runs from section 200 to section 987.

title: County grievance procedure
statement: If the county treats you unfairly, you can send a complaint to the Director of your county child welfare agency. Ask the county how its grievance process works and what it covers. Citation: CDSS Manual of Policies and Procedures §31-020 (county grievance procedures). (rights_duties, Right to File a Grievance)
source_name: CDSS Manual of Policies and Procedures, Division 31, section 31-020.1 and .2; CDSS County Complaints page
source_says: Grievance procedures shall be developed to review complaints from foster parents, legal parents, guardians, and children concerning the placement or removal of a child from a foster home.
steps: The cdss.ca.gov/Portals copy of the manual was blocked, so opened the same manual at www.cdss.ca.gov/ord/entres/getinfo/pdf/cws1.PDF and read 31-020. The citation is right and parents are covered, but only for complaints about placing a child in or removing a child from a foster home. 31-020.2 lists what gets no review, for example "Removal of a child for direct placement into an adoptive home." and "Any complaint regarding only the validity of a law or of a statewide regulation." The note cites WIC 16503. The complaint-to-the-Director sentence comes from a different source, the CDSS County Complaints page (cdss.ca.gov/reporting/file-a-complaint/county-complaints): "the Director of the county CWS agency for resolution." That page does not mention 31-020. Pages were read through the web fetch tool, which returns short quoted segments.
fix: Keep the description. Change the citation to: CDSS Manual of Policies and Procedures, Division 31, section 31-020 (county grievance review for complaints about placing a child in a foster home or moving a child out of one); CDSS County Complaints page (other complaints go to the county Director).

title: Parent access to the case file
statement: You have the right to review and obtain copies of documents in your dependency case file. Citation: WIC § 827(a)(1)(D), (a)(5); Rule 5.552 and form JV-570 (only for people who are not already allowed to see the file, or for parts a judge must release). Link: selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/jcc-form/JV-570 (legal_content, How to Request Your Case File)
source_name: WIC 827(a)(1)(D), (a)(3)(A), (a)(5); Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.552(a); form JV-570 page
source_says: a case file may be inspected only by the following: ... The minor's parent or guardian. ... may also receive copies of the case file.
steps: Opened the public.law page for 827: (a)(1)(D) lists the parent, and (a)(5) lists (D) among those who "may also receive copies of the case file". (a)(3)(A): parts kept private by another law follow that law, and people without access under it "shall petition the juvenile court". Opened rule 5.552 on courts.ca.gov: "With the exception of those persons permitted to inspect juvenile case files without court authorization under sections 827 and 828, every person or agency ... must petition the court for authorization using ... (form JV-570)." Opened the JV-570 page: it is a "Petition for Access" used to "Ask the court for a court order". So a parent does not need a court order or JV-570 for the file itself. The entry text and citation are right. Its only link still goes to JV-570, which could send parents to a form they do not need. Pages were read through the web fetch tool, which returns short quoted segments.
fix: You can see and get copies of your child's court file without a court order. You do not need form JV-570. That form is for people who need the judge's permission. A judge may need to release parts that another law keeps private. Change the link so it does not point parents to JV-570.

title: Close family friend examples
statement: A neighbor or a teacher can count too, when that kind of bond is already there. (glossary_terms, Non-Relative Extended Family Member (NREFM), definition)
source_name: WIC 362.7; CDSS Kinship Care page; California Courts Self-Help Guide for relatives
source_says: an adult caregiver who has ... a familial or mentoring relationship with the child. ... The parties may include relatives of the child, teachers, medical professionals, clergy, neighbors, and family friends.
steps: Opened the public.law page for 362.7. The definition turns on the bond, not on who the adult is: "an adult caregiver who has an established familial relationship with a relative of the child ... or a familial or mentoring relationship with the child." Nothing in it leaves out a neighbor or a teacher. But the only place the section names teachers and neighbors is the next part: "The county welfare department shall verify the existence of a relationship through interviews with the parent and child or with one or more third parties." and then "The parties may include...". There they are people the county may talk to, not examples of who can qualify. The CDSS Kinship Care page and the UC Davis kin-first definitions page repeat the statute. The Self-Help Guide for relatives gives no examples. No source opened names a neighbor or teacher as an example of this kind of caregiver. Pages were read through the web fetch tool, which returns short quoted segments.
fix: Any adult with that kind of bond can count. The county checks that the bond is real by talking with the parent and child, or with people like relatives, teachers or neighbors.
